title: Grade 3 Division Word Problems: Sharing vs Grouping (+ Free Quiz)
meta_title: Grade 3 Division Word Problems + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Teach grade 3 division word problems the easy way: spot sharing vs grouping, write the number sentence and handle remainders. Free 8-question quiz inside.
excerpt: The hardest part of a division story is not the maths — it is knowing whether you are sharing or grouping. Here is how I teach Grade 3 to tell them apart, write the sentence, and cope with the bits left over, plus a quick quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Give a Grade 3 class this problem — ‘Riya has 24 laddoos and shares them equally among 6 friends’ — and most children will get 4. Change one word so it reads ‘Riya packs 24 laddoos into boxes of 6’ and the same children hesitate, even though the answer is still 4. That pause is the whole story of grade 3 division word problems. The numbers are easy; the trouble is figuring out what the story is actually asking. Once a child can name the two kinds of division problem, half the battle is won.

I have taught this to eight-year-olds for years, and the single biggest jump in confidence comes not from more sums but from a moment of sorting: is this a sharing problem or a grouping problem? Let me show you the difference, because it is the difference that matters.

The two kinds of division word problems

Every division story a Grade 3 child meets is one of two types. They look almost identical on the page, which is exactly why children mix them up.

Equal sharing (how many each?)

You know how many groups you have, and you want to know how many go in each group. ‘24 sweets shared among 6 children — how many does each child get?’ You are dealing the sweets out, one to each child, like cards. The answer, 4, tells you the size of each share.

Equal grouping (how many groups?)

You know how big each group should be, and you want to know how many groups you can make. ‘24 sweets put into bags of 6 — how many bags?’ Here you keep scooping out sixes until the pile is gone. The answer, 4, tells you the number of groups.

Same numbers, same answer, completely different picture in the child’s head. And that picture is what lets them check whether their answer makes sense.

How to spot which is which

The quickest tell is the question at the end. ‘How many each?’ is sharing. ‘How many groups / bags / boxes / rows?’ is grouping. I get children to underline the question words before they touch the numbers. It sounds slow. It saves them from the most common mistake of all — dividing the wrong way round.

  • Sharing signals: shared equally, split between, given out, how many each, divided among friends.
  • Grouping signals: packed into, put into boxes of, groups of, rows of, how many bags, how many teams.

Here is a caveat worth saying out loud to parents: in a sharing problem the divisor is the number of people; in a grouping problem the divisor is the size of each group. Get children to say what they are dividing by, in words, and the confusion melts.

Writing the division sentence

Once the type is clear, the sentence writes itself. The total always comes first, then the divide sign, then whatever we are dividing by. For ‘24 laddoos shared among 6 friends’ the sentence is 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Teach children to read it aloud as a full sentence: ‘24 divided by 6 equals 4, so each friend gets 4 laddoos.’ That last clause — naming what the 4 means — is what stops a child from writing a bare number and forgetting the units.

Use the times tables you already know

This is the part I wish more textbooks shouted about. Grade 3 children do not need a new skill to divide — they need their multiplication tables, read backwards. To solve 24 ÷ 6, a child should ask ‘6 times what makes 24?’ They already know 6 × 4 = 24, so the answer drops out. Every division fact is a multiplication fact wearing a different hat.

I keep dividends within the tables a child has learnt — up to about 100 — and divisors from 1 to 10. If a child is shaky on the 7 table, division by 7 will feel impossible, and the fix is the table, not more division drills. That is a genuinely useful diagnosis: weak division is almost always weak tables in disguise.

A gentle first look at remainders

Real life rarely divides evenly, and Grade 3 is the right time for a soft introduction. Take ‘25 chocolates packed into boxes of 6 — how many full boxes, and how many left over?’ A child counts sixes: 6, 12, 18, 24 — that is 4 full boxes — and 1 chocolate is left over. We write it as 25 ÷ 6 = 4 remainder 1.

Keep the story concrete. ‘Full boxes and leftovers’ makes far more sense to an eight-year-old than the abstract word ‘remainder’ on its own. And do ask the follow-up: could you fill another whole box? No — you only have 1 chocolate, and a box needs 6. That reasoning is worth more than the notation.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a short, free quiz built from exactly these ideas — sorting sharing from grouping, writing the sentence, using the tables, and a couple of gentle remainder questions. Let your child work through it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. quiz.title: Grade 3 Division Word Problems Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight short story problems on sharing, grouping and simple remainders. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 3 division word problems within the tables

questions.q: 24 sweets are shared equally among 6 children. How many does each child get?
questions.explanation: This is a sharing problem. 24 ÷ 6 = 4, because 6 × 4 = 24, so each child gets 4 sweets.

questions.q: A shopkeeper packs 24 apples into bags of 6. How many bags does he fill?
questions.explanation: This is a grouping problem: how many sixes are in 24? 24 ÷ 6 = 4 bags.

questions.q: Which problem is a grouping (how many groups) problem?
questions.explanation: ‘Put into boxes of 5’ tells you the group size and asks how many groups — that is grouping.

questions.q: 42 mangoes are shared equally among 7 baskets. Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: The total comes first: 42 ÷ 7 = 6, because 7 × 6 = 42. Each basket gets 6 mangoes.

questions.q: To solve 45 ÷ 9, which multiplication fact helps?
25 chocolates are packed into boxes of 6. How many are left over?
questions.explanation: 6, 12, 18, 24 fills 4 boxes and uses 24 chocolates. 25 − 24 = 1 left over.

questions.q: 56 students sit in rows of 8. How many full rows are there?
questions.explanation: This is grouping. 56 ÷ 8 = 7, because 8 × 7 = 56, so there are 7 full rows.

questions.q: 27 laddoos are shared among 4 children. How many does each get, and how many are left over?
questions.explanation: 4 × 6 = 24, so each child gets 6 laddoos. 27 − 24 = 3 left over.

faq.q: What is the difference between sharing and grouping division?
faq.a: In a sharing problem you know how many groups there are and find how many go in each — ‘24 sweets among 6 children’. In a grouping problem you know the size of each group and find how many groups — ‘24 sweets in bags of 6’. Both give 24 ÷ 6 = 4, but the picture is different.

faq.q: How do I know whether to divide or multiply in a word problem?
faq.a: Look at what is missing. If you have a total and are splitting it into equal parts, you divide. If you are combining equal groups to find a total, you multiply. The question words — ‘how many each’ or ‘how many groups’ — almost always signal division.

faq.q: Do Grade 3 children need to learn remainders?
faq.a: A gentle introduction, yes. Keep it concrete: ‘how many full boxes and how many left over’ makes sense to an eight-year-old long before the formal word ‘remainder’ does. Deep work on remainders comes in Grade 4.

faq.q: My child knows the tables but still struggles with division stories. Why?
faq.a: Almost always it is the reading, not the arithmetic. The child cannot tell what the story is asking. Practise sorting problems into sharing or grouping first, and underline the question before touching the numbers.
